patterns.title: Boolean Masking and Projection
patterns.short_description: Filters DataFrame rows using vectorized boolean conditions (&, |, ~) and selects specific column subsets or views.
mental_triggers: Select rows where age > 25 and status is active
Filter dataframe based on multiple column constraints
Subset specific columns from a large dataframe
constraint_signals: Vectorized boolean indexing avoids Python row-by-row iteration; bitwise operators &, | require parentheses around conditions
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N * C) vectorized evaluation | Space: O(M * C) filtered view/copy

patterns.title: DataFrame Merge and Join Operations
patterns.short_description: Combines two DataFrames along column keys using inner, left, right, or outer relational join semantics (pd.merge).
mental_triggers: Combine customer profiles with transaction history
Join lookup table attributes to fact records
Left join to preserve master record list with optional child data
constraint_signals: Hash join on merge keys in memory; non-unique keys produce Cartesian product on matching values
patterns.complexity: Time: O(M + N) average hash join | Space: O(M + N) merged dataframe

patterns.title: GroupBy Aggregation and Transformation
patterns.short_description: Applies split-apply-combine operations to aggregate, transform, or filter grouped records (.groupby().agg()).
mental_triggers: Calculate total and average spend per user
Find highest earner within each department
Apply custom multiple aggregation functions across different columns
constraint_signals: Split-apply-combine partitions indices; as_index=False avoids resetting index afterwards
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N) hash grouping + O(K) aggregation | Space: O(K) aggregated dataframe

patterns.title: Ranking and Row Shifting (rank and shift)
patterns.short_description: Computes dense or fractional ranks and accesses adjacent rows along an index or partition using .rank() and .shift().
mental_triggers: Find 2nd highest salary using rank(method='dense')
Compare consecutive days of stock prices using .shift(1)
Calculate lag differences between consecutive timestamp events
constraint_signals: Sorting before shifting ensures correct chronological or ordinal comparisons
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N log N) sorting + O(N) shifting | Space: O(N) series
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def rank_and_shift(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df["rank"] = df["score"].rank(method="dense", ascending=False)
    df["prev_score"] = df["score"].shift(1)
    return df

patterns.title: Handling Missing Values and Deduplication
patterns.short_description: Identifies, replaces, or drops missing (NaN / None) values and removes duplicate records based on primary key subsets.

Fill missing scores with zero or category mean

patterns.title: Vectorized String and Datetime Operations
patterns.short_description: Performs element-wise text manipulation via .str accessor and date/time decomposition and arithmetic via .dt accessor.
mental_triggers: Filter emails matching regex pattern with .str.match()
Extract year and month from timestamp column via .dt.year
Convert string timestamps to datetime objects with pd.to_datetime
constraint_signals: Vectorized .str and .dt accessors avoid slow Python loop execution over Series elements
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N * L) string operations / O(N) date conversions | Space: O(N) series
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def string_datetime(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df["clean_email"] = df["email"].str.strip().str.lower()
    df["year"] = pd.to_datetime(df["created_at"]).dt.year
    return df

patterns.title: Vectorized Conditionals and Custom Mapping
patterns.short_description: Evaluates branching conditionals using np.select() / np.where() and applies custom transformations across rows or series.
mental_triggers: Categorize numeric scores into low, medium, and high bands
Compute custom row-level conditional calculations based on multiple column flags
Avoid row-by-row iteration in favor of array-level vectorization
constraint_signals: np.select() executes in compiled C array speed; .apply(axis=1) is slow fallback for complex non-vectorizable logic
patterns.complexity: Time: O(N) vectorized array evaluation | Space: O(N) output series
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def transform_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df["bonus"] = df["salary"] * 2
    df["tier"] = np.where(df["salary"] >= 100000, "High", "Standard")
    return df

hints.title: Deriving a New Column from Existing Attributes
hints.text: Employee compensation is stored in a salary attribute. How can you calculate a doubled compensation amount for every row and attach the result as a new column labeled bonus?

hints.title: Vectorized Arithmetic Assignment Invariant
hints.text: Arithmetic operations on pandas Series operate element-wise in C without Python loop overhead, allowing direct assignment to new column names.

hints.title: Vectorized Column Creation Procedure
hints.text: Assign a new bonus column on the DataFrame set to the salary column multiplied by two. Return the updated DataFrame.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```python
import pandas as pd

def createBonusColumn(employees: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    employees['bonus'] = employees['salary'] * 2
    return employees
```

complexity.notes: Vectorized column multiplication and assignment in contiguous memory.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Using apply() with a lambda or iterating with a loop introduces heavy interpreter overhead compared to vectorized Series arithmetic.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Direct vectorized column assignment scales linearly in O(N) time and allocates an O(N) Series.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Using vectorized multiplication rather than apply(lambda x: x * 2).

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def createBonusColumn(employees: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    employees['bonus'] = employees['salary'] * 2

hints.title: Selective Column Deduplication

hints.title: Null Value Imputation
hints.text: Certain inventory records have missing numerical quantities represented as null. How can you substitute missing values in a specific attribute with zero while keeping all other values unchanged?

hints.title: Null Imputation Invariant
hints.text: Imputing missing values with a designated default preserves the total row count and replaces null tokens without mutating valid non-null entries.

hints.title: Fillna Application Procedure
hints.text: Invoke the fillna method on the quantity Series passing zero as the replacement argument. Reassign the result to the quantity column and return the DataFrame.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```python
import pandas as pd

def fillMissingValues(products: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    products['quantity'] = products['quantity'].fillna(0)
    return products
```

complexity.notes: Single pass vectorized null imputation on targeted Series.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Manual iteration checking for NaN values is slow and prone to type mismatch errors with floating point NaN representations.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Series.fillna(0) scans contiguous column memory in O(N) time with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Targeting only the specified column rather than calling fillna on the entire DataFrame.

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def fillMissingValues(products: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    products['quantity'] = products['quantity'].fillna(0)
    return products

hints.title: Filter Sort Projection Pipeline
hints.text: Finding heavy animals requires three sequential operations: filtering records where weight exceeds 100, sorting descending by weight, and projecting only the animal name.

hints.title: Boolean Indexing and Sorting Chain
hints.text: Filter rows using animals[animals['weight'] > 100], sort the resulting subset with sort_values(by='weight', ascending=False), and index [['name']] to retain a DataFrame.

hints.title: Chained Method Composition
hints.text: Chain operations seamlessly: filter with boolean indexing, apply sort_values, and extract [['name']] to yield the final single-column DataFrame.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```python
import pandas as pd

def findHeavyAnimals(animals: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return animals[animals['weight'] > 100].sort_values(by='weight', ascending=False)[['name']]
```

variables: N: number of records in animals DataFrame
complexity.notes: Filtering takes linear O(N) time followed by sorting filtered candidates in O(K log K) time where K <= N.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Manual looping and appending to lists forfeits pandas vectorized C-speed filtering and timsort capabilities.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Allocating intermediate filtered subsets requires temporary memory proportional to qualifying records.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Producing a DataFrame output with double bracket notation [['name']] rather than a 1D Series.

solutions.approach: Vectorized boolean filtering with descending sort and column projection
